b1: Yesterday you learned that a moving object can keep going after a push ends. Today, choose one object and find out what is pushing or pulling on it now.
g1: Picture a backpack hanging from a strap. Follow the strap to the bag. That contact is a clue to one force.
b2: Choose a slide lead and a scribe. The lead reads the case. The scribe draws what the group describes. Switch jobs at each discussion. Each person saves their own work.
g2: Think on your own first. When you share, ask someone to point to the object that causes each force.
b3: A force is a push or a pull. Choose the object you are studying. Then name what acts on it. A hand pushing a cart exerts a force on the cart.
g3: Say the source first, the action next, and the object last. Try it with the hand and cart.
b4: The strap pulls up on the bag. Earth pulls down on the same bag. The strap must touch the bag to pull it. Earth can pull from a distance.
g4: Find both arrows in the panel. Keep your finger on the bag as you name what causes each arrow.
b5: A sensor measures force in newtons. Its sign tells direction along a chosen axis. A negative reading still means the sensor feels a force.
g5: Mark one way as positive. Before you check the answer, decide what a reading with a minus sign tells you.
r5: The force points opposite the positive direction. Its size is the distance of the reading from zero.
b6: A book rests on a level desk. Earth pulls it down. The desk pushes it up. Draw both arrows starting at the book. Their equal sizes show that they balance.
g6: Read the notebook in the panel. If you draw a force that acts on the desk, put that arrow in a separate diagram for the desk.
b7: Tip the surface to make a ramp. Gravity still points straight down. The surface pushes outward at a right angle to the ramp. This push is called the normal force.
g7: Lay a pencil along the ramp in the picture. Turn it a quarter turn to find the direction of the surface push.
b8: The car rolls downhill with its engine off. The picture includes a force that resists its motion. Check each arrow by naming what pushes or pulls the car.
g8: Try adding an arrow just because the car moves downhill. Can you name an object that causes that extra push?
r8: Leave out the extra arrow. Motion tells which way the car travels. Every force arrow needs a real source.
b9: The Sun pulls on the asteroid through gravity. A spacecraft could also push the asteroid during a collision. Track what acts before contact, during contact, and after they separate.
g9: Read the two boxes in the panel. One describes the story now. The other describes a possible event. Keep those times separate.
b10: An engineer draws a forward push on the asteroid even after the craft leaves. Decide if that arrow belongs. Use the objects in the story to defend your choice.
g10: Ask your group which interaction has ended and which still acts. An object can keep moving after contact ends.
r10: The contact push ends when the craft leaves. The Sun still pulls. The asteroid can keep its changed motion while gravity continues to bend its path.
b11: A sign hangs still from one vertical cable. Draw the forces on the sign. Label the source and direction of each force. Use your drawing to explain why the sign stays still.
g11: Work on your own. Describe the arrows in Work so your teacher can follow your drawing. Use the timer to pace yourself.
q1: A hand lets go of a bag. Which object still pulls the bag down?
q2: A strap holds a bag still. Name two forces on the bag. For each, name its source and direction.
q3: A book rests on a ramp. Describe the direction of gravity and the direction of the ramp’s push. Explain why the arrows point different ways.
q4: A craft taps the asteroid and moves away. Explain which force ends and which force remains. Give a reason for each choice.
h: Choose one object. For each arrow, name what pushes or pulls that object.
sign: The cable pulls up and Earth pulls down. The forces balance while the sign hangs still.
p1a: Sketch the strap pulling on the bag. Explain where your arrow starts and points.
p1b: Find a force on the bag that needs no contact. Name the source and direction.
p2a: Draw gravity and the surface push on the downhill car. Use the ramp to place your arrows.
p2b: Check whether a downhill motion arrow belongs in the force diagram. Give evidence from the picture.
p3a: Sketch the forces on the asteroid while the craft touches it. Name the source of each force.
p3b: Sketch the forces after the craft leaves. Explain why one arrow should disappear.
discuss: Compare the two sketches on your whiteboard. Take turns naming the object behind each force.
reply: Choose one arrow from your classmate. Explain why you would keep, turn, or remove it.
reflect: Describe one arrow you checked. How did checking its source help you explain it?
ex1: The bag is still, so nothing pulls on it.
ex2: The ramp pushes straight up no matter how much it tilts.
ex3: The craft keeps pushing the asteroid after they separate.
crit: Check the claim against the picture. Correct the arrow and explain what causes the force.
solo: Work on your own. Read the case, check the sample claim, and save your explanation.
alt4: The strap pulls up on Maz’s bag while Earth pulls down.
alt6: Notebook diagram of upward normal force and downward weight on a book.
alt8: Car on a ramp with gravity downward, the surface push outward, and resistance uphill.
alt9: Two panels compare the Sun’s pull with possible spacecraft contact.
b12: Today you will draw an arrow for each push or pull on one object. You will explain where each arrow points and name the object that causes it.
g12: Hold your hand flat under a book. Notice which way you must push to support it. Keep that example in mind.
b13: Look at a hand holding a cup. If you study the cup, list pushes and pulls on the cup. Save forces on the hand for a different drawing.
g13: Draw a circle around the cup in your sketch. Say the last part of each label aloud: on the cup.
b14: A string pulls a toy while they touch. Earth pulls the toy even when it hangs in the air. Both forces can act on the toy at the same time.
g14: Imagine cutting the string. Decide which source can still act without touching the toy. Check your idea.
r14: Once the string stops touching the toy, its pull ends. Earth still pulls the toy toward the ground.
b15: Draw the bag as a dot. Show the strap’s pull and Earth’s pull. Ask a classmate to check the source and direction of one arrow. Then save your own idea in Work.
g15: Let the scribe draw while another person names the source. If you have approval to work alone, check the sample claim in Part 1.
t16: Turn a picture into a diagram
b16: Replace the book with a dot. Start each arrow at the dot. Draw its tip in the direction of the force. Put the name of the source beside the arrow.
g16: Cover one arrow with your finger. Use the other arrow to say who acts, on what, and in which direction.
b17: A level desk pushes up on a still book with 8 N. Earth pulls down with 8 N. Draw arrows of equal length. The two forces act even though their total is zero.
g17: Use the same scale for both arrows. Count upward as positive, then add the two signed forces.
t18: Keep the source beside the arrow
b18: A student puts the book’s push on the desk into a drawing of the book. Check the object at the end of the label. Which drawing should contain that arrow?
g18: Read the label as a sentence. The last object is the one that feels the push.
r18: The desk feels that push, so draw it on the desk’s diagram. The desk’s push on the book belongs on the book’s diagram.
b19: A sled slides down a rough ramp. The runners slide past the snow downhill, so the snow’s friction on the sled points uphill, along the surface.
g19: Trace the sled’s slide along the snow. Trace the friction arrow along the same surface in the opposite direction.
b20: Switch roles. Sketch a downhill car with its engine off. Name the source of each arrow. Compare the arrow from the road with the arrow from Earth and explain why they point different ways.
g20: Use the ramp in Part 2 of Work. Check the angle of one arrow before each person saves their reasoning.
b21: Picture the asteroid before the craft arrives. In our simple model, the Sun’s gravity is the only pull we show. Draw it toward the Sun while the two objects are far apart.
g21: Keep the asteroid as your chosen object in every sketch. Look for contact before adding a contact arrow.
b22: Imagine the craft touches the asteroid and pushes it to the right. Add a rightward contact arrow on the asteroid. Keep the Sun’s pull in the picture during the tap.
g22: Say which arrow you added and why. A new force can act while an earlier force still acts.
b23: Line up the before, during, and after pictures. Circle what changes at contact. The push can change velocity during the tap. That new velocity can outlast the push.
g23: Use one color for forces and another for velocity. Look for an arrow that tells you about motion rather than a push or pull.
t24: Test the claim on the ground
b24: A rolling ball has left a student’s hand. Another student says the hand must still push because the ball moves. Use what you learned from the spacecraft to check the claim.
g24: Point out exactly when the hand loses contact. Then name one force that can still act on the ball.
r24: The hand no longer pushes. Earth still pulls down, and the floor still pushes up while the ball touches it.
b25: Switch roles. One person draws the asteroid during the tap. Another draws it after the tap. Compare one arrow that stays and one that changes. Save your own explanation in Part 3.
g25: Use words from a classmate’s sketch to explain what you checked. If working alone with approval, check the supplied claim.
t26: Check a diagram on your own
b26: Start a fresh sketch. Mark the object. Name what touches it. Look for gravity. Check each direction. Cross out any force you cannot link to another object.
g26: Try the steps with a coat on a hook before you open the exit question. Keep your answer in your own words.
b27: Two people draw the same upward force. One uses a long arrow and one a short arrow. Compare their scales first. Within one diagram, equal forces need equal arrow lengths.
g27: Give the whiteboard one scale for everyone. Measure the arrows from the same starting dot.
b28: A picture shows an asteroid and a nearby craft. It does not show whether they touch. Explain which force you can name now and which needs more evidence.
g28: Think about what a second picture, taken a moment later, might show. A nearby object does not always touch.
g31: Connect the sensor with no load. Zero it before adding the string. Use the range and sign convention shown for this setup.
g32: Record the reading at rest and with the test mass. Keep the sign and unit. If the sign is reversed, check the sensor direction.
g33: Read the axes first. Slope tells how fast velocity changes. The area between the line and zero gives the signed change in position.
g34: Choose your body as the object. Name what supports you and what pulls you down before checking the answer.
g35: A force reading gives a size in newtons. Include the direction to describe the whole force.
g36: Choose the force name by its source. A rope pulls along its length. A supporting surface pushes at a right angle to itself.
g37: Mass goes in kilograms. Multiply mass by the given gravity value to find weight in newtons. Draw its direction toward Earth.
g38: Start with the mass and the gravity value on this slide. Predict the weight before revealing the calculation.
g39: Pick the hanging mass. Use its weight and the fact that it stays still to work out the pull from the string.
g40: Work alone. Choose the car. Name Earth and every touching object that exerts a force. State what you assume about resistance.
sensor: Record the unloaded reading and two gentle trials. For each trial, name the action and record the signed reading in newtons. Explain what a change in sign means. If using supplied readings, label them as sample data.
sensorGuide: Report the source, units and signs. Compare the unloaded reading to zero and connect the sign to the sensor axis.
sample: Approved independent example: unloaded 0.00 N, gentle pull +1.20 N, gentle push −0.80 N. These are supplied readings. Label them as sample data.
sensorA: Report your unloaded reading and one pull. Name the source, sign and unit.
sensorB: Report one push. Compare its sign with the pull and check the sensor direction.
qWeight: A 2 kg mass hangs still from one string. Use 10 N/kg for gravity. Find its weight. Name the force that balances it and give its direction.
aWeight: Earth pulls down with 20 N. The string pulls up with 20 N because the mass stays still.
labExit: A car coasts downhill with its engine off and no brakes. Describe the forces on the car, name each source, and state what you assume about resistance.
exitGuide: Earth pulls down. The road pushes perpendicular to its surface. Include resistance uphill if your model includes it. Motion alone adds no force.
